source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2024) On the Self-Verification Limitations of LLMs on Reasoning and Planning Tasks (arXiv 2402.08115)
finding: GPT-4 critiquing its own answers made results worse or no better in most domains; a sound external verifier raised them a lot. The LLM verifier had high false-negative rates.
numbers: 100 instances per domain. Standard / self-critique / sound verifier: Game of 24 5/3/38; Graph Coloring 16/2/37; Blocksworld 40/55/87; Mystery Blocksworld 4/0/8. LLM-as-verifier false positive / false negative: G24 10.4/20.7; Coloring 6.5/95.8; Blocksworld 18.55/15.48; Mystery BW 0.5/97.09.
limits: GPT-4 (2023-24 era) only; planning and puzzle domains; Blocksworld self-critique did rise 40 to 55.
agent_relevance: Gap 3/4: self-critique without a sound checker is not safe; check type matters more than number of rounds. Gate reflection on a code check.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey (arXiv 2406.01297)
finding: No prior work shows successful self-correction with feedback from a prompted LLM in general tasks. It works with reliable external feedback (code interpreter, symbolic reasoner, search) or with large-scale fine-tuning. The bottleneck is feedback generation, not refinement.
numbers: No new accuracy numbers (survey). Fine-tuning methods use 20K to 274K instances. Models in table: GPT-4 family, GPT-3.5, PaLM, Llama 2, Minerva.
limits: Survey of mostly 2023-24 models; read via fetch of the HTML (first 100000 of 144423 characters). Notes many papers skip strong baselines such as self-consistency.
agent_relevance: Gap 3/4: supports rule that reflection needs an external executable signal; also warns to compare against self-consistency at equal tokens.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location (arXiv 2311.08516)
finding: Finding the first wrong step is the hard part. With the true error location, correction helps a lot; with a weak finder it can hurt. A simulation puts the break-even for the mistake finder near 60 to 70 percent accuracy.
numbers: BIG-Bench Mistake: 2,186 PaLM 2 Unicorn traces, 5 tasks. Mistake-location accuracy: GPT-4 direct step-level 52.87, GPT-4 CoT step-level 43.40, GPT-3.5 CoT step 14.31. Oracle location, change on originally-wrong traces: +18.04 to +43.92; on originally-right traces: 0 to -11.43. Simulation: gains exceed losses at about 60-70% finder accuracy (read from figure, approximate).
limits: Threshold is from a simulation on 2023 models and read off a figure, not measured with reasoning models. Trained small classifier (PaLM 2 Otter) still too weak for backtracking.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: best available number for how reliable a check must be: roughly 60-70% accurate at locating the error, else correction loses on right answers. Use as starting gate for G2, to be re-measured.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (arXiv 2310.01798), search snippet only
finding: Search result summary confirms the known result (performance degradation after intrinsic self-correction). The search tool returned no 2025 study of reasoning models on this question.
numbers: none read this pass
limits: Snippet only. Web search budget ran out before any 2025 reasoning-model self-correction search could be run.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: stays open for direct reasoning-model replications; see d05 and d06 for indirect evidence.

source: Tsui (2025) Self-Correction Bench: Self-Correction Blind Spot in LLMs (arXiv 2507.02778)
finding: Non-reasoning models fail to fix errors in their own output that they do fix when the same error is shown as external text (blind spot). Reasoning models (R1 style) show almost none. Appending 'Wait' cuts the blind spot a lot.
numbers: 14 non-reasoning open models: blind spot 64.5% average; own errors caught 4.3-10.8%. 'Wait' appended: blind spot -89.3%, mean accuracy +156%. DeepSeek-V3-0324 mean accuracy 0.567 baseline, 0.902 with Wait; DeepSeek-R1-0528 0.908. Datasets SCLI5 286, GSM8K-SC 1,313, PRM800K-SC 448 samples; greedy, 1,024-token budget.
limits: Errors are injected or controlled test cases, not natural intrinsic self-correction on an open task; short budget; single author; LLM judges.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: partly closed. Reasoning models do re-check inside their own trace, so an outer reflect-again loop adds less for them. A cheap 'Wait' nudge matches R1-level accuracy on this bench.

source: Liu et al. (2025) Understanding R1-Zero-Like Training: A Critical Perspective (arXiv 2503.20783)
finding: Base models already show self-reflection words before RL. In DeepSeek-R1-Zero, self-reflection does not imply higher accuracy; nearly half of reflective answers were no more accurate than non-reflective ones.
numbers: Dr. GRPO 7B recipe: AIME24 43.3, mean 51.4 over five benchmarks; 1.5B: AIME24 20.0, mean 42.1. Incorrect responses were longer than correct ones (likely harder questions).
quote: self-reflection does not necessarily imply higher inference-stage accuracy
limits: Open RL recipes on Qwen2.5 math models; reflection measured by keywords.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: reflection tokens are not evidence of correction. Score reflection by whether the answer flips from wrong to right, not by length or keywords.

source: Kumar et al. (2024) Training Language Models to Self-Correct via RL (SCoRe, arXiv 2409.12917)
finding: Base Gemini models self-correct badly; prompting-only Self-Refine and offline SFT stay near zero or negative; on-policy multi-turn RL gives the first clear positive gain.
numbers: MATH, Gemini 1.5 Flash, acc@t1 / acc@t2 / delta: base 52.6/41.4/-11.2; Self-Refine 52.8/51.8/-1.0; STaR 53.6/54.0/+0.4; Pair-SFT 52.4/54.2/+1.8; SCoRe 60.0/64.4/+4.4. Base turned correct to incorrect 15.8%, SCoRe 1.4%. HumanEval Gemini 1.0 Pro: base delta +3.0, SCoRe +12.2.
limits: Requires RL training; outside our no-training scope. Gemini 1.0/1.5 only.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: independent confirmation that prompt-only intrinsic self-correction lowers accuracy (-11.2 on MATH). Shows the failure mode to guard in a scaffold: changing right answers (15.8%).

source: Madaan et al. (2023) Self-Refine (arXiv 2303.17651)
finding: Self-Refine helps on style and optimisation tasks but gives about zero gain on math reasoning because the model says nothing is wrong. Oracle triggering helps a little. Specific feedback beats generic feedback.
numbers: Math reasoning base to Self-Refine: GPT-3.5 64.1 to 64.1; ChatGPT 74.8 to 75.0; GPT-4 92.9 to 93.1. ChatGPT gave 'everything looks good' on 94% of instances. Oracle trigger: GPT-3.5 68.9, ChatGPT 76.2, GPT-4 93.8. Sentiment reversal GPT-4 3.8 to 36.2; code optimisation GPT-4 27.3 to 36.0. Iterations: marginal gain falls each round (code 22.0, 27.0, 27.9, 28.8).
limits: Authors' own results; 2023 models; tasks with soft metrics for the big gains.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: a critic that nearly always approves is a useless gate. Measure the approve rate and the flip rate of any reflect step.

source: Gou et al. (2024) CRITIC: LLMs Can Self-Correct with Tool-Interactive Critiquing (arXiv 2305.11738)
finding: Tool feedback beats the same loop with no tool on every task; without tools, weaker models can fall below baseline, stronger ones gain a little.
numbers: ChatGPT with tool vs w/o tool: HotpotQA F1 52.9 vs 46.1; AmbigNQ 74.9 vs 67.3; GSM8K 78.2 vs 77.0; TabMWP 89.0 vs 87.0; toxicity (lower better) 0.173 vs 0.339 (vanilla 0.325). Davinci-003 GSM8K w/o tool 68.3 below PoT baseline 70.1. Up to 3 to 4 correction rounds.
limits: 2023 models (davinci-003, ChatGPT); tool is search or interpreter.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: an equal-loop ablation (tool vs no tool) is what we should run. Gain from tool is 1 to 7 points on reasoning, bigger on factual QA.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Reasoning in Token Economies: Budget-Aware Evaluation of LLM Reasoning Strategies (arXiv 2406.06461)
finding: At matched budgets, plain self-consistency regularly beats more complex strategies (Reflexion, multi-agent debate, ToT) on 6 datasets. Reflexion is worst of the three. ToT wins Game of 24 only with GPT-4 and a large budget.
numbers: Cap 20 queries or 10k tokens per question; 100 questions each of GSM8K, MATH, TheoremQA, CSQA, HotpotQA, Game of 24; GPT-3.5 and GPT-4. Game of 24 GPT-4: ToT b=5 top-1 0.74 (cost $159.87), b=1 0.65 ($49.9), CoT x100 top-1 0.17; GPT-3.5: ToT b=5 0.25 vs CoT x100 0.04 top-1 but best-of-all 0.35 vs 0.46. Reflexion with oracle evaluator beat SC by a large margin; with GPT-4 evaluator it underperformed SC.
limits: 100 questions per set; 2024 models; MAD numbers only in figures.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1, 2, 8: the strongest equal-token evidence found. Any scaffold arm must beat SC at the same budget; reflection only wins with a reliable evaluator.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Language Agent Tree Search (LATS, arXiv 2310.04406)
finding: LATS beats ReAct, Reflexion, ToT and RAP on HotpotQA, HumanEval, MBPP, WebShop, but the comparison is at matched k and n, not matched tokens versus best-of-N. The LM value function is the key part.
numbers: HumanEval pass@1 GPT-4: LATS 92.7, Reflexion 91.0, base 80.1; GPT-3.5: 83.8 vs Reflexion 68.1. MBPP GPT-3.5 81.1 vs 70.0. HotpotQA EM (GPT-3.5): LATS(ReAct) 0.63, ReAct 0.32, LATS(CoT+ReAct) 0.71. Ablation: no LM value 0.37 (-0.26), no reflection 0.58 (-0.05), DFS instead of MCTS 0.42. n=5, k=50 on HotpotQA; tokens on success LATS 173,290 vs ToT 210,215.
limits: Authors' own result; no best-of-N at equal tokens; page read to 100000 of 119344 characters.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: ToT-style edge is not shown against best-of-N at equal budget. Value function (not reflection) carries the gain.

source: Koh, McAleer, Fried, Salakhutdinov (2024/2026) Tree Search for Language Model Agents (arXiv 2407.01476)
finding: On non-puzzle web tasks, best-first search in the live environment lifts success, but costs up to 20 times more LM calls. Reranking trajectories plateaus below search. Value-function quality caps the gain.
numbers: VisualWebArena GPT-4o 18.9 to 26.4; Llama-3-70B 7.6 to 16.7; WebArena GPT-4o 15.0 to 19.2. 200-task subset: budget c=0 24.5, c=5 32.0, c=20 37.0; value fn GPT-4o 1 sample 28.5, 5 samples 32.5, 20 samples 37.0, ground-truth reward 43.5, LLaVA-34B 30.0. Reranking plateaus about 30 at about 7 runs.
limits: Budget measured in search nodes and LM calls, not tokens; no plain best-of-N at the same call count beyond the reranking arm. Destructive-action risk.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: partly closed. On non-puzzle agent tasks search beats reranking at 5 or more nodes, but only with an environment that supports undo and a good value function.

source: Wu et al. (2025) Inference Scaling Laws: Compute-Optimal Inference for LLM Problem-Solving (arXiv 2408.00724)
finding: At equal FLOPs, MCTS under-performs sampling methods on MATH. Reward-balanced tree search (REBASE) beats weighted-vote sampling modestly. A 7B model with REBASE matches or beats a bigger model with sampling at lower FLOPs.
numbers: MATH500 weighted voting: Mistral-7B REBASE 45.0 at 1.36e14 FLOPs vs sampling 42.8 at 8.70e14; Llemma-7B 46.8 vs 45.5; Llemma-34B 49.2 at 7.08e14 vs 46.7 at 12.1e14. Llemma-7B MATH500 43.5 (sampling, 125.4e12) vs 46.8 (REBASE, 148.0e12). MCTS dropped from GSM8K comparison for poor trade-off.
quote: MCTS underperforms the sampling-based methods at each compute budget
limits: Math only, uses trained reward model; exact MCTS numbers are in figures.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: search edge over best-of-N at equal compute is small (1 to 3 points) and depends on a process reward model; MCTS can lose.

source: Snell, Lee, Xu, Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally (arXiv 2408.03314)
finding: Best use of test-time compute depends on problem difficulty. Easy items gain most from sequential revision; harder ones from a mix of sequential and parallel. Compute-optimal allocation matches best-of-N with up to 4 times less compute. Process-reward beam search beats best-of-N at low budgets but its edge shrinks, and it over-optimises on easy items.
numbers: MATH, PaLM 2-S*. Revisions: 64 samples compute-optimal match 256 best-of-N; PRM search: 16 match 64. Beam search worse than best-of-N on levels 1-2 at large budgets; better on levels 3-4; level 5 little progress. Sequential 'narrowly outperforms' parallel (no exact figures).
limits: Needs a difficulty estimate and a trained verifier; math only; page read to 100000 of 110425 characters.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1, 8: a difficulty-triggered switch between revise and resample is the equal-token structure to test; supports gating search on a difficulty signal.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling (arXiv 2407.21787)
finding: Coverage (any sample right) keeps rising with samples, but without an automatic verifier majority vote and reward models plateau near 100 samples. Selection, not generation, is the bottleneck.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite DeepSeek-Coder-V2: 15.9% at 1 sample to 56% at 250. MATH Llama-3-8B: coverage 82.9% at 100 samples to 98.44% at 10,000; majority vote and reward model 40.50% to 41.41%. 5 DeepSeek samples 29.62% for $10.8 vs GPT-4o single 24.00% for $39.
limits: Coverage is an upper bound; verifier-free domains need a selector.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: a checker's reliability sets how much of the coverage can be turned into answers. Code-run checks are the safe regime.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: Simple test-time scaling (arXiv 2501.19393)
finding: Forcing a reasoning model to continue with 'Wait' raises accuracy modestly and then flattens; repeated suppression of the stop token can cause loops. A tree search over a process reward model scaled better than majority voting and sequential forcing on AIME24.
numbers: s1-32B: AIME24 50.0 to 56.7 (4x Wait), 53.3 with 2x Wait; MATH500 92.6 to 93.0; GPQA Diamond 56.6 to 59.6. Training set 1,000 examples.
limits: Authors' own; AIME24 has 30 questions so 1 question is 3.3 points. Exact majority-vote numbers are in figures.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: for current reasoning models, a bounded 'Wait' continuation is the working form of self-correction; unbounded forcing loops. Matches a bounded reconsider operator.

source: Hu et al. (2025) Evaluating Memory in LLM Agents via Incremental Multi-Turn Interactions (MemoryAgentBench, arXiv 2507.05257)
finding: No memory method wins all four competencies. Long context beats most agentic memory systems when it fits; plain BM25 beats embeddings on retrieval; fancy memory scores worst on conflict resolution.
numbers: Overall: GPT-5-mini long-context 60.6, worst Cognee 20.6. Accurate retrieval: GPT-5-mini 74.4, HippoRAG-v2 65.1, BM25 60.5, Qwen3-Embedding-4B 54.7, MIRIX (GPT-4.1-mini) 63.0. Test-time learning best Claude-3.7-Sonnet long-context 53.9. Selective forgetting: all methods at most 28% on multi-hop.
quote: all methods fail on the multi-hop situation
limits: Page read to 100000 of 176102 characters; no ACT-R-style recency-frequency scoring arm was found in it. Author list not confirmed this pass.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: partly answered. Simple lexical retrieval is a strong baseline; added activation machinery has no demonstrated edge. ACT-R activation arm is still unmeasured.

source: Chhikara et al. (2025) Mem0: Production-Ready AI Agents with Scalable Long-Term Memory (arXiv 2504.19413)
finding: Extracted memory scores below full context on LOCOMO but uses about 15 times fewer tokens per query and far lower latency. Authors appear tied to the product (mem0.ai contact address).
numbers: LLM-judge J: full-context 72.90, Mem0g 68.44, Mem0 66.88, best RAG 60.97, Zep 65.99, OpenAI memory 52.90, A-Mem 48.38. Tokens per query: full-context about 26,031; Mem0 1,764; Mem0g 3,616. p95 latency: full-context 17.1 s; Mem0 1.44 s.
limits: Vendor paper; J metric uses LLM judge; MemGPT has no J score.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: the equal-token trade is clear: memory buys cost, not accuracy, in this benchmark. Accuracy per token is the right metric.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM Agents Are Experiential Learners (arXiv 2308.10144)
finding: Training-free experience reuse (extracted insights plus retrieved successful trajectories) beats ReAct, and task-similarity retrieval beats random retrieval. Insights made from reflections alone were worse than full ExpeL.
numbers: HotpotQA ReAct 28.0 vs ExpeL 39.0; ALFWorld 40.0 vs 59.0 (Reflexion about 54 at R3). Retrieval on ALFWorld: task similarity 59.0, reasoning similarity 48.5, random 42.5. Insights-only 36 (HotpotQA) and 50 (ALFWorld); retrieve-only 31 and 55. Transfer HotpotQA to FEVER: ReAct 63, ExpeL transfer 70.
limits: 100 to 134 eval tasks; no equal-total-token accounting for the experience-gathering phase; text says 40 where table says 39.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: supports the caching idea and retrieval by task similarity; leaves the payback at equal total tokens unmeasured.

source: Foundation Agents survey, 48 authors (2025) Advances and Challenges in Foundation Agents (arXiv 2504.01990)
finding: A 48-author brain-inspired survey of agent memory, reasoning, self-evolution and safety. The part read (table of contents and preface) does not mention Soar or ACT-R and gives no numbers.
numbers: none
limits: Only first 100000 of 468617 characters read, mostly contents; cannot say what it concludes on gaps.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: no independent confirmation or refutation of Fan and Lan's five residual gaps found. Gap stays open.
